paper_metadata.title: Improving the Sequence Alignment Method by Quantum Multi-Pattern Recognition

summary: The paper proposes a hybrid sequence-alignment method that uses a Grover-like quantum multi-pattern recognition routine to identify matching diagonals in dot-matrix plots. The example uses EMBL DNA sequences (XL23808 and XLRHODOP), 4750 diagonal datasets of length 1625, 50-digit fragments, and about 32 repeated search applications, with a claimed 100% success probability when the learning set exceeds 1/3 of the patterns; the classical comparison is more than 7.2×10^6 computing steps.

experiments.description: Hybrid sequence-alignment method that converts dot-matrix sequence alignment into repeated applications of a Grover-like quantum multi-pattern recognition algorithm to identify matching diagonal regions between two biological sequences.

algorithm.variant: Quantum multi-pattern recognition adapted from Grover-like search

hyperparameters.success_probability: 100% when learning pattern set exceeds 1/3 of total patterns
hyperparameters.pattern_set_fraction_threshold: n + s < 2^i and success maximized near 1/3 of total patterns

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial state |φ0⟩ prepared by encoding the learning pattern set into a uniform superposition over pattern and spurious states

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Binary patterns and spurious states are encoded as basis states; each diagonal of the dot matrix is treated as a one-dimensional binary dataset of length equal to the target pattern length
problem_formulation.objective_function: Identify one or more matching diagonal regions in a dot-matrix sequence alignment by recognizing pattern states with the quantum search procedure
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Pattern set and spurious set satisfy s = n and s + n < 2^i; the method uses padding for shorter diagonals

problem_instance.description: Pairwise sequence alignment using dot-matrix plots; example application on DNA sequences from EMBL, with a long vertical sequence divided into smaller fragments of 50 digits each

dataset_specification.description: DNA sequence dot plot for XL23808 and XLRHODOP; example figure from European Molecular Biology Laboratory

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Dot-matrix recurrence plot constructed; shorter diagonals padded to equal length; long sequence split into 50-digit pieces for repeated search
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Illustrative example application; no statistical benchmarking or repeated-run protocol reported

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical dot-matrix assembly / local sequence alignment after quantum recognition
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Construct dot-matrix plot; encode diagonals as binary datasets; split long sequence into fragments
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Assemble identified diagonals with classical methods for local sequence alignment

classical_baselines.method_name: classical dynamic programming / classical dot matrix technique

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical dynamic programming / dot matrix alignment
speedup_claims.conditions: for large sequences; when the learning pattern set is close to 1/3 of total patterns and the search is applied to diagonal datasets
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper provides a complexity comparison and an illustrative example, not an empirical runtime benchmark on quantum hardware.

speedup_claims.factor: approximately 32 runs for the example application
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical alignment over the full sequence pair
speedup_claims.conditions: vertical sequence split into 50-digit pieces; about 1 search iteration per data section
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a paper-estimated number of repeated search applications, not a measured runtime.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Polynomial time; search iterations T ≅ (π/4) * sqrt(N/n)
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: Approximately 32 runs for the example application; about 1 search iteration per 50-digit data section
complexity_analysis.total_operations_classical: More than 7.2×10^6 computing steps for the example stated in the paper

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not reported; no device, simulator, qubit count, or circuit-level resource data are given.
limiting_factors: No quantum hardware or simulator execution reported
No empirical runtime benchmark on quantum devices
Quadratic Grover-like speedup only, which is not enough to establish practical advantage under Hoefler-style constant-factor analysis
Heavy data preparation and fragmentation required for long sequences
Classical postprocessing is still needed to assemble alignments

notes: The paper does not report an actual quantum device, simulator, qubit count, gate counts, or shot count; hardware and low-level circuit resources are therefore not specified.
The method is described as hybrid because quantum recognition is followed by classical local sequence alignment, but no implementation framework is named.
The paper presents a Grover-like quantum multi-pattern recognition method for sequence alignment and compares it only against classical complexity, not against a quantum implementation on hardware.

Reported numbers are illustrative: 100% success probability when the learning pattern set exceeds 1/3 of total patterns, about 1 iteration per 50-digit data section, 32 repeated applications for the example, and more than 7.2e6 classical computing steps.
